title-group.article-title: Group 1 innate lymphoid cells protect liver transplants from ischemia-reperfusion injury via an interferon-γ-mediated pathway

abstract.p: As important immune regulatory cells, whether innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) are involved in liver transplantation (LT) remains unclear. In a murine orthotopic LT model, we dissected roles of ILCs in liver ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI). Wild type (WT) grafts suffered significantly higher IRI in Rag2-γc double knockout (DKO) than Rag2 KO recipients, in association with downregulation of group 1 ILCs genes, including IFN-γ. Antibody-mediated ILC depletion or IFN-γ neutralization in Rag2 KO recipients increased, while IFN-γ treatment in DKO recipients reduced, liver graft injuries. At the donor side, grafts from DKO mice or anti-NK1.1-treated WT mice suffered significantly higher IRI, while grafts treated with IFN-γ during cold preservation decreased IRI. Thus, both recipient and donor group 1 ILCs protect liver grafts from IRI. Low-dose IFN-γ upregulated c-FLIP expression in vitro and in vivo, and protected hepatocytes from inflammatory cell death. In human liver graft biopsies, single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis revealed group 1 ILCs produce IFN-γ. The c-FLIP levels were positively correlated with IFN-γ in pre-transplant biopsies. Grafts with higher c-FLIP were associated with lower caspase-8 activation, IRI gradings, and frequency of early allograft dysfunction post-LT. Our study reveals a novel IFN-γ-mediated cytoprotective role of group 1 ILCs in LT.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), first described in 2008, are a heterogeneous lymphocyte population that originate from the common lymphoid progenitor but lack antigen-specific receptors1. The development of ILCs is recombination-activating gene (RAG)-independent, but IL-2 receptor γ chain dependent. They are the innate counterparts of effector T cells with similar diverse functional subsets. ILCs can be broadly classified into three subtypes based on effector cytokines and lineage defining transcriptional factors: group 1 ILCs, including natural killer cells (NK cells)/type 1 ILCs (ILC1s), ILC2s, and ILC3s, which mirror CD4+ T helper (Th)1, Th2, and Th17 cells, respectively2, 3. Due to their fully differentiated functional status and tissue residency, they sense the microenvironment changes and respond immediately through cytokine secretion, acting as one of the first responders in orchestrating an effective tissue immune response.

Liver is an organ enriched with ILCs, particularly ILC1s. In humans, ILC1s comprise greater than 30% of liver-resident lymphocytes (6% in mice), as compared with 2% in the peripheral blood4. ILC2s and ILC3s, although rare, are also present in livers and can expand in the disease condition5, 6. ILCs have been shown to regulate the pathogenesis of multiple types of acute and chronic liver diseases. ILC1s orchestrate type 1 response by producing interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), which activate macrophages and other immune cells to elicit pro-inflammatory responses. They can also dampen tissue inflammation by restraining T cell responses via PD-L1 and competing for IL-2 availability7, 8. More recently, ILC1s were demonstrated to protect mice from drug-induced acute liver injury via IFN-γ-mediated upregulation of Bcl-xL in hepatocytes9.

Innate immune-dominated hepatic sterile inflammation drives ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) in liver transplantation, leading to early allograft dysfunction (EAD), as well as acute and chronic rejection10, 11. Currently, severe donor organ shortage prompts the increasing usage of ‘marginal’ donor livers, which are particularly susceptible to IRI, leading to poor transplant outcomes10–12. The contribution of ILCs in organ IRI has been reported with contradicting results13–16. While early studies demonstrated that NK cells infiltrated the kidney and exacerbated renal IRI17, anti-inflammatory and pro-regenerative effects of NK cells have also been reported18. IL-33 has been shown to drive ILC2s and RORγt+ IL-22-producing NKp46+ cells to protect kidney and liver from IRI13, 14, 16. ILC1s were reported to promote liver IRI15.

In the present study, we dissected roles of ILCs in a well-established mouse orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT) model with extended donor liver cold storage to mimic clinical marginal donor livers19. We compared ILC-proficient Rag2 knockout (KO) and ILC-deficient Rag2-γc double KO mice as either recipients or donors and utilized antibodies to deplete group 1 ILCs or neutralize their functional cytokines. Our results showed that both recipient’s and donor’s group 1 ILCs protect OLTs from IRI, through an IFN-γ-mediated hepato-cytoprotective pathway.

sec.title: Clinical liver transplant study
sec.p: All human studies were approved by the UCLA Institutional Research Board (IRB protocol 13-000143 and 18-000216), and written informed consent was received from participants before inclusion in the study. We performed a retrospective analysis of 60 adult patients who underwent OLT (May 2013-August 2015) and received routine standard-of-care and immunosuppressive therapy. Recipients who underwent re-transplantation were excluded. Donor livers, procured from donation after a brain or cardiac death, were stored in UW solution (Niaspan; Bristol-Meyers Squibb, Princeton, NJ). Pre-transplant and post-transplant Tru-Cut needle biopsies from the left liver lobe were obtained after cold storage at the back table (before implantation) and about 2 h after portal reperfusion (before abdominal closure). Hepatic biopsies were screened by quantitative reverse-transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) with GAPDH normalization for IFN-γ, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1), CXCL10, CD68, Cathepsin G and by western blots with β-actin normalization for c-FLIP, Bcl-xL and caspase-8 expression. Gene expression of IFN-γ was evaluated in 51 patients. Cold ischemia time was defined as the time from the perfusion of the donor liver with UW solution to its removal from the cold storage for implantation. Warm ischemia time was defined as the time from removal from cold storage to establishing liver graft reperfusion. Recipient blood was collected before transplant and at postoperative days (POD) 1–7. Liver injury was evaluated by serum aspartate transaminase (AST) and alanine transaminase (ALT) levels. The incidence of EAD was defined by the presence of one or more of the following variables: bilirubin level of ≥10 mg/dL on POD 7, prothrombin time-international normalized ratio ≥1.6 on POD 7, or AST and ALT levels of >2000 IU/L within the first 7 POD20. Single-cell transcriptomes in human donor liver biopsies were collected from the Gene Expression Omnibus database (GSE171539) and analyzed.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: All animal experiments were approved by the UCLA Animal Research Committee (ARC 2005-006). WT, Rag2 KO, and Rag2-γc DKO mice, purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, ME), were on a C57BL/6 background and studied at 8–11 weeks of age. As the donor and recipient sex might affect transplant outcomes21, 22, we use male mice in this study.

Animals were housed in the UCLA animal facility under pathogen-free conditions. They received humane care according to the criteria outlined in the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (National Academies Press, 2011).

sec.title: Mouse OLT model and liver cold storage
sec.p: We used a mouse model of liver cold storage followed by OLT, as described by our group19. To mimic marginal human OLT, donor livers were stored in UW solution (4°C/18h) and transplanted to syngeneic recipients. In the current study, we used a syngeneic OLT combination to investigate hepatocellular injury without the confounding effects of allorejection. Liver graft and plasma samples were collected 6 h after reperfusion, the peak of hepatocellular damage in this model. The sham group underwent the same procedures except for OLT.
Supplementary files include further details of materials and methods.

sec.title: Recipient’s ILCs protect OLTs from IRI
sec.p: To determine whether ILCs were involved in OLT, we transplanted syngeneic WT C57BL/6 liver grafts into Rag2 KO vs. Rag2-γc DKO recipients after extended cold storage (Fig. 1A)19. Liver graft injury, assessed by Suzuki’s histological score23 and plasma AST/ALT levels, was significantly higher in the DKO than Rag2 KO recipients at 6h post-OLT, the peak of liver injury in this model (Fig. 1B–D). Immunofluorescence staining of liver tissue showed increased numbers of TUNEL positive cells in the DKO vs. Rag2 KO recipients (Fig. 1B, C). These results indicate that recipient’s ILCs, which are present in the RAG KO, but not DKO mice, protected OLT from IRI. To further establish the role of ILCs in Rag2 KO recipients, we administered anti-CD90.2 antibodies in Rag2 KO recipients to deplete ILCs24. The depletion of CD90.2+ cells was confirmed by FACS (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Indeed, ILCs depletion exacerbated liver graft injury in Rag2 KO recipients and diminished the difference between Rag2 KO and Rag2-γc DKO recipients (Fig. 1B–D). Collectively, our data indicates that recipient’s ILCs protected OLTs from IRI.

sec.title: Group 1 ILCs protect OLTs from IRI via IFN-γ
sec.p: To determine the molecular basis of the ILC-mediated protective mechanism, we measured expression of ILCs-associated cytokines and transcription factors in the grafts. Our results showed that IFN-γ and transcriptional factor T-box expressed in T cells (T-bet), associated with group 1 ILCs (NK/ILC1s), were significantly lower in the grafts of ILC-deficient DKO or anti-CD90.2-treated Rag2 KO recipients vs. Rag2 KO counterparts (Fig. 1E). No differences were detected in ILC2-associated IL-5, IL-13, ST2, GATA3 or ILC3-associated RORγt among these groups (Fig. 1F, G). Although anti-CD90.2 increased IL-17 levels in Rag2 KO recipient, there was no difference in ILC3-associated IL-17 or IL-22 levels between Rag2 KO and DKO recipients (Fig. 1G). These results indicated that group 1 ILCs might protect OLTs from IRI in Rag2 KO recipients. As the prototype functional cytokine of NK/ILC1s, IFN-γ levels were significantly higher in Rag2 KO than DKO recipients, as measured by ELISA (Supplementary Fig. 2A). Interestingly, there were no differences in inflammatory IL-12, TNF-α, MCP-1, or CXCL10 transcript levels among different transplant groups (Supplementary Fig. 2B). NK1.1 immunofluorescence staining of OLTs revealed that the numbers of NK1.1 positive cells were significantly higher in Rag2 KO recipients than in sham livers, indicating that group 1 ILCs infiltrated into the transplanted livers (Supplementary Fig. 2C). This increase of NK1.1 infiltration was not detected in the DKO and diminished in anti-CD90.2 treated-Rag2 KO recipients (Supplementary Fig. 2C).

To confirm that group 1 ILCs were responsible for the protection of OLTs from IRI, we treated Rag2 KO recipients with either anti-NK1.1 or anti-IFN-γ antibodies prior to OLT (Fig. 2A). Both treatments exacerbated liver graft injury in Rag2 KO recipient, as evidenced by higher Suzuki’s histological score, increased numbers of TUNEL-positive cells, elevated AST/ALT levels (Fig. 2B–D). These results indicate that NK/ILC1s protect OLTs from IRI by producing IFN-γ in Rag2 KO recipients. Immunofluorescence of NK1.1 confirmed that the number of NK1.1+ cells (NK/ILC1s) in liver grafts was significantly reduced by the anti-NK1.1, but not by the anti-IFN-γ treatment in Rag2 KO OLT livers (Fig. 2E).

sec.title: IFN-γ alleviates hepatocellular injury following OLT
sec.p: To confirm the cytoprotective effect of IFN-γ in OLTs, we administered recombinant IFN-γ in Rag2-γc DKO recipients immediately after reperfusion (Fig. 3A). As IFN-γ can increase inflammatory gene expressions25, we titrated IFN-γ doses by measuring IL-12 and TNF-α transcript levels in liver grafts. Indeed, high-dose IFN-γ (20 U/g) significantly increased intragraft IL-12 and TNF-α expression and failed to protect OLTs from IRI in Rag2-γc DKO recipients (Fig. 3B–D). Low-dose INF-γ (4 U/g), however, did not increase intragraft IL-12 and TNF-α expression (Fig.3 B, C), but protected OLTs from IRI (Fig.3 E, F). Thus, IFN-γ could protect OLTs from IRI in Rag2-γc DKO recipients.

In vitro, we tested whether INF-γ could protect hepatocytes from inflammatory cell death. Primary hepatocytes were pre-treated with low-dose IFN-γ (25 U/ml, by the titration experiment described in the Supplementary Fig. 3 A, B) followed by TNF-α/actinomycin. Hepatocellular injury, evaluated by cell death assay, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release, and AST/ALT levels in culture supernatants at 12h post-stimulation, was significantly reduced in IFN-γ primed ones vs. controls (Fig. 4 A–E). Western blots analysis at 12h post stimulation revealed that anti-apoptotic protein c-FLIP levels were significantly higher in the IFN-γ-treated cells vs. controls (Fig. 4F). Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL expressions were also trending higher in these cells. Simultaneously, caspase-8 and caspase-3 activation were suppressed after IFN-γ treatment (Fig. 4F). Collectively, low-dose IFN-γ treatment protected hepatocytes from TNF-α/actinomycin D-induced cell death by upregulating anti-apoptotic c-FLIP expression.

sec.title: Donor group 1 ILCs protect OLTs from IRI.
sec.p: ILCs are tissue resident26. To determine whether donor-derived liver resident ILCs were involved in the IRI of OLTs, we transplanted liver grafts from either Rag2 KO or Rag2-γc DKO mice into Rag2-γc DKO recipients (Fig. 5A). Indeed, liver graft injury, assessed by Suzuki’s histological score, TUNEL staining, and plasma ALT levels, was significantly higher in the DKO vs. Rag2 KO donor grafts at 6h post-OLT with significantly lower intragraft IFN-γ levels (Fig. 5B–E). ILC2s- and ILC3s-associated cytokines were not statistically different between these two graft types (Fig. 5F, G). Although not reaching statistically significant, the DKO donor livers also suffered from higher IRI compared to Rag2 KO donor livers in WT recipients (data not shown).

To further study the role of donor group 1 ILCs in liver graft injury, we depleted NK/ILC1s in WT donor mice by administering anti-NK1.1 antibody prior to liver procurement and implanted NK/ILC1s-depleted donor livers into WT recipients (Fig. 5H). Group 1 ILCs-depletion in the liver graft significantly reduced pretransplant IFN-γ production and exacerbated posttransplant graft injury (Fig. 5I–L). Thus, donor-derived group 1 ILCs contribute to intragraft IFN-γ production and protection of OLTs from IRI.

sec.title: IFN-γ treatment during liver cold preservation upregulates c-FLIP expression and attenuates IRI in OLTs
sec.p: To test whether IFN-γ could protect liver grafts from IRI in immunocompetent animals, we treated WT liver grafts with low-dose IFN-γ (25 U/ml) during cold storage and transplanted into WT recipients (Fig. 6A). Compared with control grafts, IFN-γ treated grafts showed significantly less graft injuries, as evidenced by lower Suzuki’s score, less TUNEL-positive cells, and lower AST levels (Fig. 6B–D).

To validate the cytoprotective mechanism of IFN-γ in vivo, we measured c-FLIP, caspase-8, and caspase-3 expression in pre- and post-transplant liver grafts treated with IFN-γ. The IFN-γ significantly upregulated c-FLIP expression without caspase activation in cold-stored WT liver grafts and hepatocyte cultures (Fig. 6E and Supplementary Fig. 4). Notably, post-transplant caspase activation was attenuated in the IFN-γ-treated liver grafts (Fig. 6F). Thus, low-dose IFN-γ supplement in cold-storage solution upregulated pre-transplant c-FLIP and suppressed post-transplant apoptosis pathway.

sec.title: Human Group 1 ILCs produce IFN-γ in donor liver graft
sec.p: To determine whether group 1 ILCs were present in human liver grafts and produced IFN-γ, we analyzed single-cell transcriptomes from liver transplant biopsies deposited in GEO database, which were collected from one donor liver at pre-preservation, post-preservation, and post-reperfusion27. Genes encoding transcription factors (EOMES, TBX21) and effector molecules (PRF1, GZMB) associated with group 1 ILCs were used to isolate ILC1s and NK cells (Fig. 7A–D)28. EOMES−/PRF1high cells were identified as ILC1s, whereas cells that expressed TBX21, PRF1, or GZMB were labeled as NK cells (Fig. 7E). Quantification of cell types revealed increased counts of ILC1s at post-reperfusion relative to pre-preservation and post-preservation, whereas a reduction in NK cells was observed at post-reperfusion relative to pre-preservation and post-preservation (Fig. 7F). Following labeling, cell transcriptomes were evaluated for IFN-γ expression (Fig. 7G). Indeed, elevated expression of IFN-γ was detected in ILC1s and NK cells relative to non-group 1 ILCs (Fig. 7H), suggesting that IFN-γ is produced primarily by group 1 ILCs in human OLT.

sec.title: The pre-transplant c-FLIP and IFN-γ levels and their clinical indications in human OLT
sec.p: To study the clinical relevance of our findings, we analyzed a cohort of 60 human pre- and post-transplant liver graft biopsies. Among these patients, gene expression of IFN-γ in pre-transplant liver grafts was evaluable in 51 patients (Fig. 8A). Intragraft gene expression profiling revealed that IFN-γ transcript levels were positively correlated with c-FLIP protein levels in pre-transplant biopsies (r=0.3075, P<0.05) (Fig. 8B). A trend of positive correlation was also detected between pre-transplant IFN-γ and Bcl-xL expression (r=0.2456, P=0.127) (Fig. 8B). Patients were then divided into c-FLIP low (n=26) and high (n=25) expression groups (based on the median Western blot-assisted c-FLIP levels, Fig. 8C), and compared OLT outcomes. No significant differences were found in the patients’ demographic data and clinical parameters between the two groups in both recipients or donors (Supplementary Table 1A, B). As c-FLIP protein can inhibit caspase-8-mediated extrinsic apoptosis pathway29, we assessed post-transplant caspase-8 activation in c-FLIP low vs. high groups. Representative Western blots of pre-transplant c-FLIP and post-transplant caspase-8 are shown in Fig. 8D (case# 1, 2: low c-FLIP, case# 3,4: high c-FLIP). Consistent with the mouse results, higher pre-transplant c-FLIP expression inhibited post-transplant caspase-8 activation in human OLT livers (Fig. 8 D, E).

Next, we evaluated IRI grading in human OLT, as previously reported30. Representative H&E and TUNEL staining of IRI-negative (grade=0 or 1) and IRI-positive (grade=2–4) patients are shown (Fig. 8F). c-FLIP expression was higher in the IRI-negative group than in the IRI-positive group (Fig. 8G). Conversely, c-FLIP high patients showed a trend of lower IRI grading than c-FLIP low patients (Supplementary Fig. 5A). Strikingly, the incidence of EAD tended to be lower in the c-FLIP high vs. low group (P=0.075) (Fig. 8H), although the difference was not statistically significant due to the limited number of patients. Thus, higher IFN-γ and c-FLIP expressions in pre-transplant livers might be indicative of better OLT outcomes with lower caspase-8 activation and less IRI following reperfusion. Interestingly, there were no significant differences in the mRNA levels of MCP-1, CXCL10, CD68, and cathepsin G in OLT livers between the low and high c-FLIP groups (Supplementary Fig. 5B), suggesting that pre-transplant c-FLIP exerted cytoprotection independent of innate inflammatory activation during the early OLT phase.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our study demonstrated, for the first time, the protective function of IFN-γ-producing group 1 ILCs (NK/ILC1s) of both donor and recipient origin in OLT. Taking advantage of Rag2 KO and Rag2-γc DKO mice as either donors or recipients, we determined that both donor (tissue-resident ILCs) and recipient (circulating NK cells) group 1 ILCs were involved in OLT. The translational potential of our finding was tested in the IFN-γ treatment studies both in vivo post-transplant and ex vivo during liver graft preservation. The clinical relevance of our experimental results was demonstrated by using two sets of human liver transplant cohorts. The single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis demonstrated that NK/ILC1s were the major IFN-γ producing cells in liver grafts. Moreover, IFN-γ levels in pre-transplant liver grafts were positively correlated with c-FLIP expression, which was associated with lower post-transplant caspase-8 activation, IRI gradings, and EAD in human OLT.

IFN-γ is a well-known proinflammatory cytokine to activate type 1 immune responses31. Our results here indicate that IFN-γ produced by group 1 ILCs is cytoprotective. We hypothesize that the levels of IFN-γ might be a critical determinant of its effect on liver IRI. We found that high-dose IFN-γ could increase inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-12 and TNF-α, in Rag2-γc DKO OLT recipients (Fig. 3B, C). As IFN- receptor is expressed by all types of cells, and hepatocytes are the most abundant cells in livers, low-dose IFN-γ may limit its action on hepatocytes, while higher dose of IFN-γ may activate other types of liver cells, including macrophages. Additionally, different IFN-γ levels may initiate different signaling pathways in cells. Our in vitro study using primary mouse hepatocytes revealed that high-dose IFN-γ activated caspase-3, while low-dose preferentially induced anti-apoptosis molecule c-FLIP without caspase activation (Supplementary Fig. 3A, B). Thus, IFN-γ might regulate tissue inflammatory response in dose- and cell-type dependent manners.

IFN-γ is produced primarily by T cells and NK/ILC1s. In WT mice, activated T (both CD4 and CD8) cells are the major producers. Indeed, our data showed that plasma IFN-γ concentration was much higher in WT (T cells+, B cells+, ILCs+) than Rag2 KO (T cells−, B cells−, ILCs+) recipients (Supplementary Fig. 2A). Thus, the cytoprotective effect of IFN-γ was most evident in RAG2 KO mice, but not WT mice, due possibly to the dose specific effect of the cytokine. In the clinical setting, immunosuppressive drugs, such as calcineurin inhibitors, inhibit T cell activation and IFN-γ production in transplant recipients32. Whether the drug also inhibits innate lymphocytes and their production of IFN-γ remains to be determined. Our study indicates that low levels of IFN-γ is required to maintain tissue homeostasis in livers, and total blockade of IFN-γ, although anti-inflammatory, may be detrimental to OLTs.

Similar cytoprotective effect of IFN-γ have been recently reported in an acute liver injury model with slightly different mechanistic details. ILC1s protected mice from CCL4-induced hepatocellular damage via IFN-γ secretion, which upregulated anti-apoptotic Bcl-xL in hepatocytes9. Our study showed that IFN-γ induced c-FLIP rather than Bcl-xL in hepatocytes and cold stored-liver grafts (Fig. 4F and 8B). c-FLIP inhibits extrinsic apoptosis pathway by blocking caspase-8 activation and protects hepatocytes from inflammatory cell death33, 34. TNF-α activates the extrinsic apoptosis pathway via the death receptor TNFR1 and is critical in IR-induced liver graft injury35, 36. Thus, induction of c-FLIP would effectively suppress hepatocyte apoptosis in OLT. It remains to be determined whether additional anti-inflammatory properties of IFN-γ may be involved in protecting OLTs from IRI. IFN-γ was shown to upregulate PD-L1 in cancer cells and promote tumor growth37 and also to increase the frequency of CD4+CD25+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells38. These mechanisms may potentially reduce pro-inflammatory immune activation and enhance cytoprotective/tissue reparative functions.

In the previous study, we have shown that CD4+ T cells in the donor and recipient exacerbate posttransplant liver injury39. As both Th1 CD4+ T cells and group 1 ILCs produce IFN-γ, we assessed the correlation between pretransplant IFN-γ/c-FLIP and CD4 levels. Contrary to our expectation, pretransplant liver grafts with high IFN-γ and c-FLIP showed significantly lower CD4 expression (Supplementary Fig. 5C). These results support our findings in the single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis that group 1 ILCs, rather than CD4+ T cells, might be a primary producer of IFN-γ in the pretransplant liver grafts. In addition, high IFN-γ and c-FLIP pretransplant liver grafts showed lower posttransplant CD4 expressions even after the reperfusion (Supplementary Fig. 5D), which is consistent with our previous study demonstrating that low CD4 levels in early postreperfusion phase are associated with lower liver injury. Further studies should clarify how group 1 ILCs and CD4+ T cells contribute to the pathogenesis of liver IRI.

In the machine perfusion era, there is a window of opportunity to treat donor grafts prior to transplantation. We tested the therapeutic potential of ex vivo IFN-γ treatment during liver cold preservation. We found that IFN-γ adjunct during cold storage upregulated c-FLIP expression in liver grafts and hepatocytes (Fig. 6E and Supplementary Fig. 4), resulting in suppression of post-transplant caspase activity and TUNEL-positive cells in OLT livers (Fig. 6C, F). Thus, enhanced c-FLIP expression in cold-preserved liver grafts by IFN-γ could inhibit post-transplant hepatocyte apoptosis. As group 1 ILCs comprise more than 30% of liver-resident lymphocytes in humans, vs. 6% in mice4, group 1 ILCs may play a more prominent role in human than mouse liver transplantation. Indeed, in agreement with our experimental data, we detected a significant correlation between IFN-γ and c-FLIP expression levels in pre-transplant liver biopsies, and that high c-FLIP in pre-transplant livers was associated with reduced post-transplant caspase-8 activation, IRI gradings, and incidence of EAD in human OLT (Fig. 8B, D–H).

This study has certain drawbacks. We used Rag2 KO and Rag2-γc DKO recipient mice to investigate the role of group 1 ILCs and IFN-γ in liver transplantation. These mice completely lack mature T cells and B cells. In human liver transplantation, the adoptive immunity is partially suppressed by the posttransplant immunosuppressants. Therefore, further studies should be conducted in WT mouse recipients using immunosuppressants to evaluate the effect of group 1 ILCs. Second, the human cohort size is relatively small, which limits the power of the correlation analyses. As we use needle biopsies for human liver samples, some samples are not sufficient for us to perform PCR and/or Western blots analyses, which further reduces the sample size. As to the single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis, we have used the available one deposited in the public domain. We will validate the finding when more data is available.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated that group 1 ILCs protected OLTs from IRI via IFN-γ-mediated pathway. IFN-γ upregulates c-FLIP expression, which can suppress caspase-8 activation and inhibit hepatocyte apoptosis upon inflammatory stimulation. Our results also suggest that calibrated-low-dose IFN-γ treatment in OLT recipients or during liver graft storage might be a promising therapeutic strategy to reduce IRI and improve OLT outcomes.

caption.title: Innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) alleviate liver graft injury in Rag2 KO recipients.
caption.p: (A) Mouse WT livers, stored for 18 h at 4°C, were transplanted into syngeneic WT, Rag2 deficient (KO), Rag2-γc double KO (DKO), or Rag2 KO with anti-CD90.2 recipients (n=5/group). Plasma and liver samples were analyzed at 6 h post-reperfusion. The sham group (n=5) underwent the same procedures except for orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT). (B) Representative H&E and TUNEL staining. Green indicates TUNEL positive cells and blue indicates nuclei. Scale bars=100μm. (C) Suzuki’s histological grading of liver ischemia reperfusion injury (IRI) and quantification of TUNEL cells/high power field (HPF). (D) Plasma aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (U/L). (E−G) qRT-PCR-assisted detection of mRNA coding for group 1 innate lymphoid cells (NK cell and type 1 ILCs; NK/ILC1s)-associated IFN-γ and T-box expressed in T cells (T-bet) (E), type 2 ILCs (ILC2s)-associated IL-5, IL-13, ST2, and GATA3 (F), type 3 ILCs (ILC3s)-associated IL-17, IL-22, and RORγt (G) in sham and OLT groups (n=5/group). Data were normalized to hypoxanthine guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) gene expression. Data are shown as mean ± SEM. *P<0.05, **P<0.01, ***P<0.001, ****P<0.0001, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s honestly significance difference (HSD) test.

caption.title: Anti-NK1.1 and anti-IFN-γ antibodies exacerbate liver graft injury in Rag2 KO recipients.
caption.p: (A) Mouse WT livers, stored for 18 h at 4°C, were transplanted into syngeneic Rag2 KO, Rag2-γc double KO (DKO), Rag2 KO with anti-NK1.1, or Rag2 KO with anti-IFN-γ recipients (n=4−5/group). Plasma and liver samples were analyzed at 6 h post-reperfusion. (B) Representative H&E and TUNEL staining. Scale bars=100μm. (C) Suzuki’s histological grading of liver IRI and quantification of TUNEL cells/HPF. (D) Plasma AST and ALT levels (U/L). (E) Representative (3 areas of n=4−5/group) immunostaining of NK1.1 and quantification of NK1.1+ cells in sham and OLT livers. Scale bars=100μm. Data are shown as mean ± SEM. **P<0.01, ***P<0.001, ****P<0.0001, one-way ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test.

caption.title: Low-dose IFN-γ treatment (4 U/g) mitigates liver graft injury in Rag2-γc double KO (DKO) recipients.
caption.p: (A) Mouse WT livers, stored for 18 h at 4°C, were transplanted into Rag2-γc DKO recipient treated with or without IFN-γ (n=3−5/group). Plasma and liver samples were analyzed at 6 h post-reperfusion. (B, C) qRT-PCR-assisted detection of IL-12 and TNF-α in OLT. Data were normalized to HPRT gene expression. (D) Plasma AST levels (U/L). (E) Representative H&E/TUNEL staining and Suzuki’s histological grading of liver IRI and quantification of TUNEL cells/HPF. Scale bars=100μm. (F) Plasma AST levels (U/L). Data are shown as mean ± SEM. *P<0.05, **P<0.01, one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD test (B−D), Student’s t-test (E, F).

caption.title: IFN-γ treatment protects hepatocytes against TNF-α-induced cell death.
caption.p: (A) Primary hepatocytes isolated from WT mouse were pretreated with 25 U/ml of IFN-γ prior to actinomycin D/TNF-α-induced cell injury. (B) Representative images of dead cell detection at 0 h (n=3), 6 h (n=6), and 12 h (n=6) of actinomycin D/TNF-α treatment in WT hepatocytes with or without INF-γ. Arrowheads indicate dead cells. Scale bars=100μm. (C) Quantification of dead cells. (D) LDH levels (U/L) and (E) AST/ALT levels (U/L) in hepatocyte culture medium (0 h: n=3, 6 h: n=6, 12 h: n=6). (F) Western blot-assisted detection and relative intensity ratio of c-FLIP/β-actin, Bcl-2/β-actin, Bcl-xL/β-actin, cleaved caspase-8/procaspase-8, and cleaved caspase-3/procaspase-3 in naive and actinomycin D/TNF-α-treated hepatocytes with or without IFN-γ (n=3−4/group). Data are shown as mean ± SEM. *P<0.05, **P<0.01, ****P<0.0001, Student’s t-test.

caption.title: Donor Group 1 ILCs increase IFN-γ in the liver grafts and protect OLTs from IRI.
caption.p: (A) Mouse Rag2 KO or Rag2-γc DKO donor livers, subjected to extended cold storage (18 h at 4°C), were transplanted into Rag2-γc DKO recipients (n=5/group). Plasma and liver samples were analyzed at 6 h post-reperfusion. (B) Representative H&E and TUNEL staining in OLT livers. Scale bars=100μm. (C) Suzuki’s histological grading of liver IRI and quantification of TUNEL cells/HPF. (D) Plasma ALT levels (U/L). (E−G) qRT-PCR-assisted detection of mRNA coding for group 1 ILCs (NK/ILC1s)-associated IFN-γ and T-box expressed in T cells (T-bet) (E), type 2 ILCs (ILC2s)-associated IL-5, IL-13, ST2, and GATA3 (F), type 3 ILCs (ILC3s)-associated IL-17, IL-22, and RORγt (G) in OLT groups (n=5/group). Data were normalized to HPRT gene expression. (H) NK1.1+ cell-depleted mouse WT livers, stored for 18 h at 4°C, were transplanted into syngeneic WT recipients (n=5−6/group). Liver samples were analyzed after cold storage (before implantation), and plasma/liver samples were analyzed at 6 h post-reperfusion. (I) Representative (3 areas of n=5 in WT and n=4 in WT+anti-NK1.1 antibody) immunostaining of NK1.1 and quantification of NK1.1+ cells in WT liver with or without anti-NK1.1 antibody. Scale bars=100μm. (J) qRT-PCR-assisted detection of IFN-γ in 18 h cold-stored WT livers with or without anti-NK1.1 antibody (n=4/group). Data were normalized to HPRT gene expression. (K) Representative H&E staining and Suzuki’s histological grading of liver IRI in OLT. Scale bars=100μm. (L) Plasma AST levels (U/L). Data are shown as mean ± SEM. *P<0.05, **P<0.01, ***P<0.001, ****P<0.0001, Student’s t-test (C−G, I−L)

caption.title: IFN-γ supplement in cold-stored liver grafts enhances pre-transplant c-FLIP expression and alleviates post-transplant graft injury.
caption.p: (A) Mouse WT livers, stored for 18 h at 4°C with or without IFN-γ (25 U/ml), were transplanted into syngeneic WT recipients (n=5−6/group). Liver samples were analyzed after cold storage (before implantation), and plasma/liver samples were analyzed at 6 h post-reperfusion. (B) Representative H&E and TUNEL staining in OLT livers. Scale bars=100μm. (C) Suzuki’s histological grading of liver IRI and quantification of TUNEL cells/HPF. (D) Plasma AST levels (U/L). (E) Western blot-assisted detection and relative intensity ratio of c-FLIP/β-actin, cleaved caspase-8/procaspase-8, and cleaved caspase-3/procaspase-3 in naive and cold-stored livers (n=3/group). (F) Western blot-assisted detection and relative intensity ratio of cleaved caspase-8/procaspase-8 and cleaved caspase-3/procaspase-3 in sham and OLT groups (n=3−4/group). Data are shown as mean ± SEM. *P<0.05, **P<0.01, ***P<0.001, Student’s t-test (C, D, F), one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s HSD test (E).

caption.title: Human liver group 1 ILCs produce IFN-γ during peri-transplant period.
caption.p: (A−D) UMAP of liver biopsy cells overlaid with expression of EOMES, TBX21, PRF1, and GZMB. (E) Cell types inferred from genes in (A−D). (F) Quantification of ILC1s and NK cells by biopsy time-point. (G) UMAP of liver biopsy cells overlaid with expression of IFN-γ. (H) IFN-γ expression distributions for non-group 1 ILCs, NK cells, and ILC1s.

caption.title: Pre-transplant liver c-FLIP positively correlates with IFN-γ expression and is associated with lower post-transplant caspase-8 activation, hepatic IRI, and early allograft dysfunction (EAD) in human OLT.
caption.p: (A) Pre-transplant (after cold storage) and post-transplant (2h after reperfusion) hepatic biopsies were collected from OLT patients. Pre-transplant liver gene expressions of IFN-γ were available in n=51 patients. (B) Relationship between pre-transplant IFN-γ gene expression and c-FLIP/Bcl-xL protein expression assessed by Western blots. Data were normalized to GAPDH gene and β-actin protein expression. (C) Pre-transplant liver grafts were divided into low (n=26) vs. high (n=25) c-FLIP expression groups, based on the median value of relative c-FLIP/β-actin levels (cut-off=1.4). (D) Representative Western blots of hepatic pre-transplant c-FLIP and post-transplant caspase-8 (case 1/2: low c-FLIP, case 3/4: high c-FLIP levels). (E) Western blot-assisted detection and relative intensity ratio of post-transplant cleaved caspase-8/procaspase-8 in low and high pre-transplant c-FLIP groups. c-FLIP were normalized to β-actin protein expression. (F) Representative H&E and TUNEL staining of IRI (−) grade=1 and IRI (+) grade=3 patient. Scale bars=100μm. (G) Pre-transplant c-FLIP expression evaluated by Western blots with β-actin normalization in IRI (−) and IRI (+) groups. (H) Incidence of EAD in OLT patients. Data are shown as mean ± SEM. *P<0.05, non-parametric Spearman’s method (B), Mann-Whitney U test (E and G), Fisher’s exact test (H).
